intro: Eight cases that get harder as you go, across the anus, esophagus, rectum, pancreas, and liver. Each starts with a one-liner, then gives you more information step by step: the exam, endoscopy, MRI, and PET, the stage, where radiation fits around surgery and chemo, the dose and targets, the landmark trials, and the side effects and follow-up. Some steps are multiple choice, some are fill-in-the-blank.

cases.title: Case 1: Not Hemorrhoids
cases.oneLiner: A 58-year-old woman has had 6 months of anal bleeding and pain, treated as hemorrhoids. Exam finds a firm 3.5 cm mass in the anal canal. Her groins feel normal.

steps.label: Workup
steps.caption: A carcinoma of the anal canal on exam, easy to mistake for a hemorrhoid. Dr. K.-H. Günther, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0.
steps.prompt: Biopsy shows squamous cell carcinoma. Which set of tests comes next?
choices: CT chest/abdomen/pelvis ± PET/CT, pelvic MRI, an HIV test, and a gynecologic exam
No staging needed; go to surgery
steps.explanation: Anal cancer is HPV-driven, so check HIV and screen the cervix. MRI defines the primary and pelvic nodes; PET/CT finds groin and distant disease. Always examine the groins.

steps.label: Stage
steps.context: MRI: 3.5 cm anal canal tumor invading the internal sphincter; vagina clear. PET/CT: no nodal or distant disease. HIV negative.
steps.prompt: What are the T and N stage?
steps.answer: T2 N0
steps.explanation: Anal T stage is size: T1 2 cm or less, T2 over 2 and up to 5 cm, T3 over 5 cm, T4 invades adjacent organs (vagina, urethra, bladder), whatever the size. Sphincter invasion does not count as T4.

steps.label: Treatment
steps.prompt: What is the treatment?
choices: Definitive chemoRT: IMRT with 5-FU (or capecitabine) and mitomycin; surgery only for salvage
steps.explanation: Anal cancer is the one GI site where chemoRT, not surgery, is the cure, and most patients keep their sphincter. APR is saved for persistent or recurrent disease.

steps.label: Trial
steps.prompt: Which trial showed that mitomycin with 5-FU and RT beat induction plus concurrent cisplatin?
steps.explanation: Nigro first showed chemoRT could replace APR. RTOG 9811 favored mitomycin, and ACT II confirmed cisplatin was no better and maintenance chemo didn't help.

steps.label: Dose
steps.caption: Elective nodal CTV (yellow) for anal cancer on axial CT slices, from L5 down to the inguinal nodes. Dapper H et al., BMC Cancer 2019 (PMC6664500), CC BY 4.0.
steps.prompt: Give the RTOG 0529 doses for her T2 N0 tumor.
steps.answer: Primary 50.4 Gy in 28 fractions; elective nodes (inguinal and pelvic) 42 Gy in 28 fractions.
steps.explanation: Every patient has the groins and pelvic nodes treated, even when node-negative.

steps.label: Response
steps.prompt: Eight weeks after chemoRT, a small firm area is still felt. What do you do?
choices: Keep watching: responses can keep improving up to 26 weeks after starting; biopsy only if it persists or grows
steps.explanation: ACT II showed many complete responses only appear by 26 weeks. Operating too early leads to unnecessary APRs.

steps.label: Side effects
steps.prompt: What side effects do you counsel her about?
steps.answer: Acute: a severe skin reaction in the perineum and groins, diarrhea, painful urination, fatigue, and low counts from mitomycin. Late: fibrosis, vaginal narrowing and sexual dysfunction (dilators), infertility and early menopause, bowel urgency, and pelvic insufficiency fractures.
steps.explanation: Avoid treatment breaks: they lower cure rates.

cases.title: Case 2: Food That Won't Go Down
cases.oneLiner: A 63-year-old man with obesity and long-standing heartburn has 3 months of trouble swallowing solids and a 12 lb weight loss.

steps.label: Background
steps.caption: Barrett's esophagus: salmon-colored columnar mucosa extending above the GE junction (arrows mark the top of the gastric folds). Japan Esophageal Society, Esophagus 2017 (PMC5222925), CC BY 4.0.
steps.prompt: Upper endoscopy shows salmon-colored mucosa reaching up from the GE junction and a mass at 36-41 cm. What is the precursor, and what cancer type is most likely?
steps.explanation: Reflux and obesity drive Barrett's metaplasia and distal adenocarcinoma. Smoking and alcohol drive squamous cell carcinoma, usually higher in the esophagus.

steps.label: T stage
steps.caption: High-frequency EUS of a normal esophageal wall with a schematic of its layers. Yun SM et al., J Korean Soc Radiol 2024 (PMC11473974), CC BY-NC 4.0.
steps.prompt: Which test best defines the T stage?
steps.explanation: EUS shows the wall layers and nearby nodes. PET/CT checks for distant disease.

steps.label: Stage
steps.context: EUS: tumor through the muscularis into the adventitia; 2 periesophageal nodes. PET/CT: avid primary and nodes, no distant disease. HER2 negative, MMR proficient. Fit for surgery.
steps.prompt: What is his clinical stage?
steps.answer: cT3 N1 M0 adenocarcinoma
steps.explanation: Through the muscularis into the adventitia is T3; 1-2 regional nodes is N1.

steps.label: Trial
steps.prompt: Which trial established 41.4 Gy in 23 fractions with weekly carboplatin and paclitaxel before esophagectomy, nearly doubling median survival?
steps.explanation: CROSS gave a pCR rate of 29% overall (49% in squamous cell). For adenocarcinoma, perioperative FLOT is an alternative; ESOPEC found better survival with FLOT than CROSS.

steps.label: Dose
steps.prompt: Give the CROSS dose and a key lung constraint.
steps.answer: 41.4 Gy in 23 fractions with weekly carboplatin and paclitaxel; keep lung V20 under about 20% to limit lung complications after surgery.
steps.explanation: Heart dose matters too for distal tumors.

steps.label: After surgery
steps.prompt: After CROSS and esophagectomy, the specimen still has residual cancer. What is added?
steps.explanation: CheckMate 577 showed better disease-free survival with adjuvant nivolumab for residual disease after neoadjuvant chemoRT and surgery.

steps.label: Side effects
steps.prompt: What side effects during chemoRT should you plan for?
steps.answer: Esophagitis (painful swallowing from about week 2-3) with weight loss, so nutrition support (sometimes a feeding tube), plus fatigue and low counts; later, lung and heart effects.

cases.title: Case 3: The Low One
cases.oneLiner: A 54-year-old man has 2 months of rectal bleeding. Colonoscopy finds an adenocarcinoma 4 cm from the anal verge. It is MMR proficient.

steps.label: Imaging
steps.caption: T2 MRI of a low rectal cancer in three planes: extramural venous invasion (red arrows), and tumor deposits (green) vs a malignant node (blue). Curcean S et al., Cancers 2024 (PMC11394290), CC BY 4.0.
steps.prompt: Which study best stages the primary?
steps.explanation: Rectal MRI shows the depth of spread, the distance to the mesorectal fascia (MRF), EMVI, nodes, and the relation to the sphincters. CT chest/abdomen/pelvis checks for metastases.

steps.label: Stage
steps.context: MRI: T3c tumor, lower edge 4 cm from the verge, 0.5 mm from the MRF, EMVI positive, 3 suspicious mesorectal nodes. CT: no metastases. CEA 6.
steps.prompt: Summarize the stage and the high-risk features.
steps.answer: cT3c N1b M0 (stage III) with a threatened MRF, EMVI, and a low location.
steps.explanation: MRF 1 mm or less is threatened. EMVI and a low tumor raise the risk of local and distant recurrence.

steps.label: Approach
steps.prompt: Which approach is best?
choices: Total neoadjuvant therapy (chemoRT plus about 4 months of chemo), then TME or watch-and-wait
steps.explanation: High-risk rectal cancer gets total neoadjuvant therapy. Long-course chemoRT is preferred for a threatened MRF or T4.

steps.label: Trial
steps.prompt: Which trial first showed that preoperative chemoRT beat postoperative chemoRT, cutting local recurrence (6% vs 13%) with less toxicity?
steps.explanation: The German rectal trial made neoadjuvant treatment the standard. RAPIDO and PRODIGE 23 then supported total neoadjuvant therapy; OPRA showed organ preservation; PROSPECT allowed selective RT omission for lower-risk tumors.

steps.label: Dose and nodes
steps.caption: Axial T2 MRI of a T3 rectal cancer reaching the left mesorectal fascia. Pikūnienė I et al., Cureus 2023 (PMC10493462), CC BY 4.0.
steps.prompt: Give the long-course chemoRT dose and the nodes you would cover.
steps.answer: 45 Gy to the pelvis with a boost to 50.4-54 Gy (28-30 fractions) and capecitabine; cover the tumor, the whole mesorectum, and the presacral, internal iliac, and obturator nodes.
steps.explanation: Add external iliac nodes for T4 tumors into anterior organs, and inguinal nodes if the anal canal is involved.

steps.label: Restaging
steps.caption: Restaging T2 MRI after treatment: a dark, fibrotic full-thickness scar (arrow) with no regrowth on 4-year follow-up. Ortega CD, Perez RO, Insights Imaging 2019 (PMC6542937), CC BY 4.0.
steps.prompt: After TNT, endoscopy shows a flat white scar and MRI shows only dark fibrosis. What option does he have?
choices: Watch-and-wait with close MRI and endoscopy surveillance, keeping his rectum
steps.explanation: A clinical complete response allows watch-and-wait. In OPRA, about half of patients kept their rectum; regrowth, usually in the first 2 years, is salvaged with TME.

steps.label: Late effects
steps.prompt: If he had a low anterior resection instead, what bowel problem would you warn him about?
steps.answer: Low anterior resection syndrome: urgency, frequency, clustering, and incontinence, worse after pelvic RT. Other late effects: sexual and urinary dysfunction and infertility (sperm banking before treatment).

cases.title: Case 4: The Groin Node
cases.oneLiner: A 51-year-old man with HIV (CD4 520, undetectable viral load) has a 6 cm anal canal cancer and a firm 2.5 cm left groin node.

steps.label: HIV
steps.prompt: How does his HIV status change treatment?
choices: He gets standard chemoRT, since his CD4 count is good and HIV is controlled
steps.explanation: Well-controlled HIV patients get standard chemoRT. Keep antiretrovirals going and watch counts closely.

steps.label: Stage
steps.context: PET/CT: 6 cm avid anal canal tumor; avid 2.5 cm left inguinal node (FNA positive); no external iliac or distant disease.
steps.caption: Fused FDG PET/CT of anal cancer in another patient: (a) primary, (b) avid inguinal node, (c) external iliac node. Koppula BR et al., Cancers 2022 (PMC9179927), CC BY 4.0.
steps.prompt: What is his TNM stage and group?
steps.answer: T3 N1a M0, Stage IIIC
steps.explanation: Over 5 cm is T3. Inguinal, mesorectal, or internal iliac nodes are N1a; external iliac N1b; both N1c.

steps.label: Treatment
steps.prompt: Which treatment?
choices: Definitive chemoRT with 5-FU or capecitabine plus mitomycin
steps.explanation: Node-positive anal cancer is still treated with definitive chemoRT.

steps.label: Doses
steps.prompt: Give the RTOG 0529 doses for the primary, the involved node, and the elective nodes.
steps.answer: Primary 54 Gy in 30; involved node 3 cm or less 50.4 Gy in 30 (over 3 cm, 54 Gy); elective nodes 45 Gy in 30.
steps.explanation: Dose painting with IMRT spares the skin, bowel, bladder, and genitals compared with older 3D plans.

steps.label: Acute toxicity
steps.prompt: Which acute side effect drove the move to IMRT in RTOG 0529?
choices: Severe skin, GI, and GU toxicity and blood count drops (with fewer treatment breaks on IMRT)
steps.explanation: IMRT reduced severe skin and GI toxicity compared with older techniques, which helps patients avoid breaks.

steps.label: Eight months later
steps.prompt: Eight months later he has new pain in his lower back and hip when walking; there is no sign of recurrence. What late effect should you consider, and what else would you counsel him about?
steps.answer: A pelvic insufficiency fracture (sacrum or pubic rami) from RT to the pelvic bones. Also counsel on sexual dysfunction, infertility (sperm banking before treatment), bowel urgency, and skin fibrosis.
steps.explanation: MRI or CT shows the fracture; it is usually managed conservatively.

cases.title: Case 5: Not a Surgical Candidate
cases.oneLiner: A 72-year-old heavy smoker and drinker with severe COPD has trouble swallowing. Endoscopy finds a mid-thoracic esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (27-33 cm).

steps.label: Bronchoscopy
steps.prompt: Bronchoscopy is ordered. Why?
choices: To rule out tracheal or bronchial invasion or a fistula
steps.explanation: Mid- and upper-thoracic tumors sit right behind the trachea and left main bronchus. Airway invasion (T4b) or a fistula changes the plan.

steps.label: Biology
steps.caption: Coronal CT (A) and FDG PET/CT (B) of a mid-esophageal cancer (white arrows) with avid nodes. Tashiro H et al., Surg Case Rep 2025 (PMC12702577), CC BY 4.0.
steps.prompt: PET/CT shows a 6 cm tumor with a subcarinal node and no distant disease; the airway is clear. What is special about squamous cell carcinoma and chemoRT?
steps.answer: Squamous cell carcinoma is more radiosensitive (pCR about 49% with CROSS vs about 23% for adenocarcinoma), so definitive chemoRT is a real curative option.

steps.label: Treatment
steps.prompt: He is a poor surgical candidate. What is the treatment?
steps.explanation: RTOG 8501 showed chemoRT beat RT alone for esophageal cancer.

steps.label: Trial
steps.prompt: Which trial showed that raising the dose to 64.8 Gy was no better than 50.4 Gy?
steps.explanation: Definitive chemoRT for esophageal cancer uses 50-50.4 Gy.

steps.label: Constraints
steps.prompt: Which organs at risk matter most for a mid-esophageal plan?
steps.answer: Lungs (especially with his COPD: keep V20 and mean lung dose low), heart, spinal cord, and, for distal tumors, the liver and kidneys.

steps.label: Follow-up
steps.prompt: Six months later he has trouble swallowing again, but endoscopy shows a narrow, smooth segment with no tumor. What is it?
choices: A benign radiation stricture, treated with dilation
steps.explanation: Strictures are a common late effect of esophageal chemoRT. Biopsy any mass or ulcer, since recurrence can look similar.

cases.title: Case 6: Yellow Eyes
cases.oneLiner: A 66-year-old man has painless yellowing of his eyes and skin, dark urine, pale stools, and a 10 lb weight loss.

steps.label: Workup
steps.caption: Scleral icterus (yellow eyes) from jaundice. CDC/Dr. Thomas F. Sellers, Wikimedia Commons, public domain.
steps.prompt: CT shows dilated bile and pancreatic ducts (a 'double duct sign'). Which study should be done next to judge resectability?
choices: Pancreatic-protocol (multiphase) CT, ideally before a biliary stent
steps.explanation: Painless jaundice with a double duct sign is pancreatic head cancer until proven otherwise. A pancreatic-protocol CT defines vessel contact; stents can blur the picture, so image first when possible. EUS gives tissue.

steps.label: Resectability
steps.caption: Portal venous phase CT of a hypoenhancing pancreatic head mass (red arrow) next to the SMV, with a biliary stent. Louis M et al., Cureus 2025 (PMC11981547), CC BY 4.0.
steps.prompt: CT shows a 3 cm pancreatic head mass with 200° of SMV contact and a short narrowed segment that can be reconstructed, no arterial contact, and no liver lesions. What category?
steps.explanation: Vein contact over 180° or narrowing that can still be reconstructed is borderline. Over 180° arterial encasement (SMA, celiac) or an unreconstructable vein is locally advanced.

steps.label: Plan
steps.prompt: What is the plan?
steps.answer: Biliary stent for the jaundice; neoadjuvant mFOLFIRINOX (± chemoRT or SBRT); restage; then a Whipple with vein resection if feasible, followed by more chemo.
steps.explanation: Germline testing is done for every pancreatic cancer (BRCA status changes systemic options).

steps.label: Trial
steps.prompt: Which trial showed that adjuvant mFOLFIRINOX after resection improved median survival (about 54 vs 35 months)?
steps.explanation: Chemo leads in pancreatic cancer. LAP07 showed chemoRT for locally advanced disease improved local control but not survival; PREOPANC supported neoadjuvant chemoRT.

steps.label: SBRT
steps.prompt: If SBRT is used, what dose range, and which organs limit it?
steps.answer: About 33-40 Gy in 5 fractions; the duodenum, stomach, and bowel right next to the pancreas (bleeding, ulcer, perforation) limit the dose.

steps.label: Palliation
steps.prompt: If the disease had been unresectable with severe back pain, which RT option helps pain?
choices: RT to the tumor and celiac plexus region
None; RT never helps pancreatic pain
steps.explanation: Pancreatic pain often comes from tumor at the celiac plexus; RT to that region (or a celiac plexus block) can relieve it.

cases.title: Case 7: The Surveillance Ultrasound
cases.oneLiner: A 64-year-old man with hepatitis C cirrhosis (Child-Pugh A6) has a new 4 cm liver lesion on his routine surveillance ultrasound. His AFP is 180.

steps.label: Diagnosis
steps.caption: Multiphase CT of HCC in another patient: (A) arterial hyperenhancement, (B) washout on the delayed phase, with tumor extending into the right portal vein. Han JE et al., J Liver Cancer 2021 (PMC10035689), CC BY-NC 4.0.
steps.prompt: Multiphase MRI shows arterial hyperenhancement, washout, and a capsule. What is the next step?
steps.explanation: In a cirrhotic liver, classic arterial enhancement plus washout (LI-RADS 5) is diagnostic of HCC; biopsy is not required.

steps.label: Staging
steps.context: MRI: 4 cm segment VII HCC abutting the IVC, not suited to ablation; no vascular invasion or extrahepatic disease. Resection declined (portal hypertension). Transplant evaluation is under way.
steps.prompt: What BCLC stage is he, and why does Child-Pugh matter for RT?
steps.answer: BCLC A (single tumor, preserved liver function, performance status 0). Child-Pugh A (to B7) patients can get SBRT with a lower risk of liver toxicity.
steps.explanation: Liver function, not just the tumor, decides what can be offered.

steps.label: Option
steps.prompt: Which is a reasonable radiation option?
choices: SBRT, for example as a bridge to transplant
No RT is ever used for HCC
steps.explanation: SBRT is used for tumors not suited to ablation, as a bridge to transplant, and for portal vein tumor thrombus. TACE and Y-90 are other liver-directed options.

steps.label: Trial
steps.prompt: Which trial showed that adding SBRT to sorafenib improved overall and progression-free survival in unresectable HCC?
steps.explanation: RTOG 1112 made SBRT a real option for HCC.

steps.label: Dose
steps.prompt: Give an SBRT dose range and the normal liver constraint.
steps.answer: About 30-50 Gy in 3-5 fractions; keep at least 700 cc of normal liver under 15 Gy (and respect stomach and duodenum limits).

steps.label: Toxicity
steps.prompt: Two months after SBRT he develops ascites, an enlarged liver, and a rising alkaline phosphatase, without tumor progression. What is it?
steps.explanation: RILD usually appears weeks to a few months after RT, with anicteric ascites and hepatomegaly. Poor baseline liver function raises the risk, which is why Child-Pugh and liver dose limits matter.

cases.title: Case 8: The Family History
cases.oneLiner: A 38-year-old woman whose mother had endometrial cancer at 46 and whose uncle had colon cancer at 42 has a mid-rectal adenocarcinoma, cT3 N1.

steps.label: Key test
steps.prompt: Which test result would most change her treatment?
steps.explanation: MMR-deficient (MSI-high) rectal cancers respond dramatically to checkpoint inhibitors, which can replace chemoRT and surgery.

steps.label: Syndrome
steps.context: MRI: mid-rectal T3b tumor, MRF clear, 2 mesorectal nodes. IHC: loss of MSH2/MSH6 (MMR-deficient).
steps.caption: Axial T2 MRI of two rectal cancers with the mesorectal fascia traced: (a) T3ab with the MRF clear, (b) T3cd reaching the MRF. Bogveradze N et al., Insights Imaging 2023 (PMC9849549), CC BY 4.0.
steps.prompt: IHC shows loss of MSH2 and MSH6 (MMR-deficient). Which syndrome should she be tested for?
steps.explanation: Young age, a family history of colorectal and endometrial cancer, and an MMR-deficient tumor all point to Lynch syndrome. Her relatives can be tested, and she needs endometrial and ovarian cancer risk management too.

steps.label: Trial
steps.prompt: Which study showed that dostarlimab alone produced complete clinical responses in essentially every patient with MMR-deficient locally advanced rectal cancer?
steps.explanation: Every patient in the Cercek study had a clinical complete response and avoided radiation and surgery, at least initially.

steps.label: First treatment
steps.prompt: What is her first treatment?
steps.explanation: Checkpoint inhibitor first for dMMR rectal cancer, with close MRI and endoscopic surveillance.

steps.label: If incomplete
steps.prompt: If she didn't respond fully to immunotherapy, what would come next?
steps.answer: Standard chemoRT or TNT, then TME; radiation and surgery are still available.

steps.label: Why it matters
steps.prompt: She is 38 and hopes to have children. Why is avoiding pelvic RT so valuable for her?
steps.answer: Pelvic RT would likely cause ovarian failure and infertility (and affect the uterus), plus sexual, bowel, and bladder late effects. Immunotherapy alone avoids these.
steps.explanation: If pelvic RT were needed, fertility preservation (egg or embryo freezing, ovarian transposition) would be discussed first.
